# When a Square Fills In: The Hidden Algebra of Discrete Loops

## A hole you can hear

Take a piece of string, tie its ends together, and drop the loop onto a
tabletop. Nothing interesting happens — you can slide the loop around, shrink
it to a point, and it never gets stuck. Now put a coffee mug in the middle of
the table and loop the string around its handle. Suddenly the loop is trapped.
No amount of sliding will contract it to a point without cutting the string or
lifting it over the handle. The loop has *detected a hole*.

This is the oldest idea in topology: a space is interesting precisely when it
has loops that cannot be contracted. The collection of all such loops, with a
rule for combining them, forms a group — the **fundamental group** — and it is
one of the most powerful fingerprints a shape can have. A disk has a trivial
fundamental group (every loop shrinks). An annulus, a donut, a figure-eight
each have their own richer fundamental groups that count and combine holes in
different ways.

For a century this theory lived in the continuous world of rubber sheets and
smooth deformations. But the objects we actually compute with — networks,
meshes, images, the cells of a simulation — are *discrete*. They are made of
vertices, edges, and higher building blocks glued along their faces. A natural
and surprisingly subtle question arises: **can we define "a loop that cannot be
contracted" using nothing but combinatorics, and get an invariant that behaves
like the classical one?**

This article is about a clean, fully rigorous answer to that question for one
of the most useful families of discrete spaces: **cubical sets**, spaces built
not from triangles but from squares, cubes, and their higher-dimensional
analogues. We will define a **discrete fundamental group**, watch it detect a
hole in an empty square, and then watch that hole vanish the instant we fill
the square in. Along the way we will meet a single principle that governs the
entire phenomenon: *filling can only create contractions, never destroy them.*

## Building spaces out of squares

A **cubical set** is a recipe for gluing together cubes of every dimension. In
dimension zero we have **vertices** (points). In dimension one we have
**edges** (segments) connecting vertices. In dimension two we have **squares**
(the 2-cubes), each with four boundary edges. In higher dimensions we have
solid cubes, hypercubes, and so on. Cubical sets are the natural language of
grids, of digital images (whose pixels are literally little squares), and of
many models in geometry and computer science, because products of cubes are
again cubes — a convenience that triangulations do not enjoy.

For the story of loops we only need the low-dimensional part of the picture,
the so-called **1-truncated** cubical set: its vertices and edges (together
called the **1-skeleton**) and its squares. A **loop** is a walk along edges
that starts and ends at the same vertex. Two loops should count as "the same"
if one can be deformed into the other by sliding across the squares that are
present. The whole subtlety is packed into that last clause: *which squares are
present.* A loop that runs around the boundary of a square can be slid across
the square and contracted — but only if the square is actually filled in. If
the square is missing, the loop is stuck, exactly like the string around the
mug handle.

## Turning geometry into a group presentation

Here is the key move that makes everything computable. To describe loops
algebraically, we use a classical bookkeeping trick.

First, choose a **spanning tree** of the 1-skeleton: a collection of edges that
connects every vertex without forming any loop of its own. Traveling along tree
edges never takes you around a hole, so we declare every tree edge to be
"trivial" — the identity. Every remaining (non-tree) edge becomes a **generator**:
a basic loop you are allowed to use.

Second, each **square** that is filled in contributes a **relation**. Reading
its four boundary edges in order spells a word in the generators — the square's
**boundary word** — and filling the square declares that this word equals the
identity. Geometrically: "the loop around this square can be contracted, so it
counts as nothing."

The resulting object — generators (the edges), modulo relations (tree edges are
trivial; boundary words of filled squares are trivial) — is a **presented
group**. We call it the **discrete fundamental group** and write it $\pi_1^{A}$.
Two loops are **discretely homotopic** (deformable into one another) exactly
when they represent the same element of this group. This is the synthetic,
combinatorial definition of "a loop that cannot be contracted," and it needs no
rubber sheets at all.

## The empty square remembers; the filled square forgets

The smallest experiment that reveals the whole phenomenon uses a single square
with four boundary edges. Label them $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$. Choose a spanning
tree consisting of the three edges $e_0, e_1, e_2$, so those three are set to
the identity, leaving one honest generator: $e_3$, the edge that closes the
loop.

**Case 1: the hollow square.** Suppose the square is *not* filled — we have its
four edges but no 2-cell spanning them. Then the only relations are the three
tree relations $e_0 = e_1 = e_2 = 1$. The presented group is therefore free on
the single generator $e_3$: it is a copy of the integers $\mathbb{Z}$. This is
not a technicality; it is the heart of the matter. **The hollow square has a
nontrivial discrete fundamental group.** Concretely, there is a homomorphism
from the group onto $\mathbb{Z}$ that sends $e_3$ to $1$ — a "winding number"
that counts how many times a loop wraps around the missing square. Because that
homomorphism sends $e_3$ to something nonzero, $e_3$ cannot be trivial, and the
group cannot collapse. The hole is real, and the algebra sees it.

**Case 2: the filled square.** Now glue in the 2-cell. This adds exactly one new
relation: the boundary word $e_0 \, e_1 \, e_2 \, e_3 = 1$. But we already
declared $e_0 = e_1 = e_2 = 1$. Substituting, the boundary relation collapses to
$e_3 = 1$. The last surviving generator dies. Every generator is now trivial,
and so **the entire discrete fundamental group collapses to the trivial group**:
a single point's worth of loops, all contractible. The hole has been sealed.

The contrast is the punchline of discrete homotopy theory in miniature: *the
same loop* — the boundary of the square — is nontrivial when the square is
hollow and trivial when the square is filled. Two-dimensional cells are the
precise mechanism by which one-dimensional loops become contractible.

## One principle to rule them: filling only creates contractions

It would be a thin result if it only worked for one hand-built square. The real
content is a general law about how the discrete fundamental group *changes* when
you add cells.

Adding filled squares means adding relations. Suppose one cubical set's
relations form a set $R_1$ and we enlarge it to a bigger set $R_2$ by filling in
more squares, so $R_1 \subseteq R_2$. Then there is a canonical group
homomorphism
$$\varphi : \pi_1^{A}(R_1) \longrightarrow \pi_1^{A}(R_2)$$
that sends each edge generator to the corresponding edge generator, and this map
is always **surjective**. Nothing in the target is missed; every loop in the
larger complex is the image of a loop in the smaller one.

Read the surjectivity carefully, because it encodes a genuine asymmetry of
nature. A surjection can *merge* elements together (its kernel can be large) but
it can never invent elements out of nowhere. Translated back into geometry:
**filling in cells can only make more loops contractible; it can never make a
contractible loop become stuck.** Homotopy can be destroyed by filling, never
created. The hollow-versus-filled square is simply the extreme case of this law,
where the surjection from $\mathbb{Z}$ down to the trivial group crushes the
winding-number generator to nothing.

There is also a clean sufficient condition for total collapse, which we used
above: *if every edge generator becomes trivial in $\pi_1^{A}$, then the whole
group is trivial.* The reasoning is that the generators, by definition,
generate the entire group; if each of them is the identity, the subgroup they
generate is both everything and nothing at once, forcing the group to be a
single point. This is the algebraic face of the statement "every loop is
null-homotopic."

## Why this is more than a curiosity

The picture we have drawn — generators are edges, relations are squares,
filling collapses loops — is a faithful, fully rigorous shadow of the classical
theory, and it comes with three attractive features.

**It is genuinely combinatorial.** Everything is a finite manipulation of words
in generators. There are no limits, no continuity, no deformation retracts to
verify by hand. A computer can carry out the bookkeeping, and the winding-number
homomorphism can be evaluated by simply counting signed occurrences of an edge
in a word.

**It is functorial.** The subset law $R_1 \subseteq R_2 \Rightarrow$ surjection
is not an accident of one example; it is a structural principle that turns the
discrete fundamental group into a well-behaved invariant that *transforms
predictably* as you build a space up cell by cell. This is exactly the property
that makes an invariant useful rather than merely defined.

**It points upward.** The same template — generators, then relations, then
relations-among-relations — is the ladder that classical algebra climbs to reach
higher homotopy. In our setting the rungs are literal cubes: edges give
generators, squares give relations, and solid cubes should give the relations
among relations that compute the *second* discrete homotopy group. The boundary
of a hollow solid cube ought to behave like a two-dimensional sphere, detecting
a higher hole, while a fully filled cube should be contractible. The
one-dimensional theory pinned down here is the base of that ladder, and it fixes
the pattern for every step above it.

## The shape of things to come

Once you believe that filling a square kills a loop, a cascade of bold,
testable conjectures follows. Attaching an $n$-dimensional cube to a space that
is already connected in lower dimensions should induce a surjection on the
$(n-1)$-st discrete homotopy group whose kernel is generated by the boundary of
the new cube — while leaving all the lower homotopy untouched. Cubes, in other
words, are surgical: they only cut holes of their own dimension and never
disturb the floors below. Symmetries of the cubes — the coordinate swaps that
make these spaces "quasisymmetric" — should act on the fundamental group by
automorphisms, so that the homotopy of a symmetric quotient is exactly the part
fixed by the symmetry. And there should be a gluing law, a discrete van Kampen
theorem, that computes the fundamental group of a space assembled from two
overlapping pieces in terms of the pieces and their overlap.

Each of these is a precise, falsifiable statement, and each rests on the same
small foundation we have laid: a square, four edges, one generator, and the
single decisive act of filling it in. The empty square remembers its hole; the
filled square forgets. From that one bit of memory, an entire discrete world of
shape and connectivity unfolds.

# Discrete Homotopy Groups of Quasisymmetric Cubical Sets: A Synthetic Model of the Fundamental Group

## Abstract

We develop a synthetic, purely combinatorial model of the discrete fundamental
group $\pi_1^{A}$ of a $1$-truncated cubical set, in the spirit of the homotopy
theory of cubical sets and the discrete homotopy theory of graphs. Given the
$1$-skeleton of a cubical set together with its two-dimensional cells, we choose
a spanning tree of the $1$-skeleton and *define* the discrete fundamental group
to be the group presented by the edge generators, modulo the relations that
collapse the tree edges and impose the boundary words of the filled squares.
Discrete homotopy of loops is precisely the congruence generated by these
relations. We prove four structural results. First, a collapse criterion: if
every edge generator is trivial in $\pi_1^{A}$, the group is trivial. Second, a
functoriality (monotonicity) theorem: an inclusion of relation sets
$R_1 \subseteq R_2$ — geometrically, filling additional squares — induces a
canonical *surjective* homomorphism $\pi_1^{A}(R_1) \twoheadrightarrow
\pi_1^{A}(R_2)$ preserving edge generators, so that filling can only create
null-homotopies and never destroy them. Third, we compute the smallest
nontrivial example: the boundary loop of a single *hollow* square is a
nontrivial element, and the group is free of rank one, i.e. isomorphic to
$\mathbb{Z}$, detected by an explicit winding-number homomorphism. Fourth, we
prove the collapse: *filling* the square with a $2$-cell trivializes the entire
group, and the filling map is a surjection onto the trivial group. Together
these results reproduce, in a fully rigorous synthetic setting, the qualitative
content of discrete homotopy theory: two-dimensional cells are the mechanism by
which loops become null-homotopic. We conclude with numerical illustrations,
algorithms for computing the invariant on small complexes, and a program of
higher-dimensional conjectures.

## 1. Introduction

The fundamental group is the most classical invariant distinguishing spaces up
to homotopy: it records the equivalence classes of based loops under continuous
deformation, with concatenation as the group operation. In the continuous
setting this invariant is defined analytically, through maps of intervals and
homotopies between them. Yet the spaces that appear in computation — grids,
meshes, digital images, discretized configuration spaces — are combinatorial
objects assembled from cells glued along faces. It is therefore natural to seek
a *synthetic* fundamental group: an invariant defined by finite combinatorial
data that nevertheless captures the homotopical content of the space.

**Cubical sets** are a particularly convenient class of such combinatorial
spaces. Instead of simplices (points, segments, triangles, tetrahedra) they are
built from *cubes*: vertices, edges, squares, solid cubes, and higher
hypercubes. Because a product of cubes is again a cube, cubical sets interact
smoothly with products and mapping spaces, which makes them the natural setting
for higher-dimensional rewriting, for digital topology (pixels and voxels are
literally cubes), and for the constructive homotopy theory that has recently
found applications in the semantics of type theory.

This paper isolates the one-dimensional heart of the theory and gives it a
complete, self-contained algebraic treatment. We work with $1$-truncated cubical
sets — vertices, edges, and squares — and we define the **discrete fundamental
group** $\pi_1^{A}$ through a group presentation obtained by the classical
spanning-tree / van Kampen bookkeeping. The definition is elementary, but the
theorems it supports are precisely the ones a good invariant should satisfy: a
collapse criterion, functoriality under cell attachment, a nontrivial base
computation, and an explicit example of a loop that is nontrivial when a square
is hollow and trivial once the square is filled.

Our contributions are:

1. A synthetic definition of $\pi_1^{A}$ as a presented group (Section 3).
2. A **collapse criterion** (Theorem 4.1): triviality of all edge generators
   forces triviality of the whole group.
3. A **functoriality / monotonicity theorem** (Theorem 5.1): filling additional
   squares induces a canonical surjection preserving generators. Homotopy can be
   created but never destroyed by filling.
4. A complete analysis of the **single-square example** (Section 6): the hollow
   square realizes $\mathbb{Z}$ (Theorem 6.1) and the filled square is trivial
   (Theorem 6.2), with the filling map an explicit surjection onto the trivial
   group (Theorem 6.3).

## 2. Cubical sets and discrete loops

We recall only the structure we need.

**Definition 2.1 (1-truncated cubical set).** A *$1$-truncated cubical set*
consists of a set $V$ of **vertices**, a set $E$ of **edges** each equipped with
a source and target in $V$, and a set $S$ of **squares** (2-cubes), each
equipped with an ordered list of four boundary edges forming a closed walk. The
pair $(V, E)$ is the **$1$-skeleton**.

**Definition 2.2 (loop).** A *loop based at a vertex $v$* is a closed edge-walk
$v \to v$, i.e. a finite sequence of edges (traversed forwards or backwards) that
begins and ends at $v$. Concatenation of loops based at $v$ is associative up to
reparametrization and admits inverses (traverse the walk backwards), so loops
based at $v$ form a group under concatenation once we quotient by the appropriate
notion of deformation.

**Definition 2.3 (discrete homotopy).** Two loops are *discretely homotopic* if
one can be transformed into the other by a finite sequence of elementary moves:
(i) cancellation of an edge immediately followed by its reverse, and (ii)
replacement of the boundary walk of a *filled* square by the trivial walk (or
vice versa). Discrete homotopy is an equivalence relation compatible with
concatenation.

The content of the theory is that Definition 2.3 has a compact algebraic
description, to which we now turn.

## 3. The synthetic discrete fundamental group

Fix a $1$-truncated cubical set. Let $\mathrm{Free}(E)$ denote the free group on
the edge set $E$; a based loop, read as a word in the edges (an edge traversed
backwards contributing the inverse letter), determines an element of
$\mathrm{Free}(E)$. Choose a **spanning tree** $T \subseteq E$ of the connected
$1$-skeleton: a maximal acyclic set of edges. Traversing a tree edge cannot
enclose a hole, so we impose the relation $e = 1$ for each $e \in T$. Each filled
square $s \in S$ contributes its **boundary word** $w_s \in \mathrm{Free}(E)$,
the product of its four boundary edges in order, and filling imposes $w_s = 1$.

**Definition 3.1 (discrete fundamental group).** Let
$$R \;=\; \{\, e : e \in T \,\} \;\cup\; \{\, w_s : s \in S \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathrm{Free}(E)$$
be the set of relators. The **discrete fundamental group** of the cubical set is
the presented group
$$\pi_1^{A}(R) \;:=\; \langle\, E \mid R \,\rangle \;=\; \mathrm{Free}(E) / \langle\!\langle R \rangle\!\rangle,$$
the quotient of the free group on the edges by the normal closure of $R$. We
write $\mathrm{of} : E \to \pi_1^{A}(R)$ for the map sending each edge to its
class (a generator), and $\mathrm{mk} : \mathrm{Free}(E) \to \pi_1^{A}(R)$ for
the induced quotient homomorphism on words.

Two loops are discretely homotopic (Definition 2.3) if and only if their words
have the same image under $\mathrm{mk}$. This is the standard spanning-tree /
van Kampen description of the fundamental group of a $2$-complex, transported to
the synthetic cubical setting; we take it as the definition of $\pi_1^{A}$.

The universal property of a presented group is the tool we use throughout: to
define a homomorphism out of $\pi_1^{A}(R)$ into a group $G$, it suffices to
specify the image of each generator $\mathrm{of}(e)$ by a function $f : E \to G$
such that every relator $r \in R$ maps to $1$ under the induced free-group
homomorphism $\mathrm{Free}(E) \to G$. We denote the resulting homomorphism
$\mathrm{toGroup}(f)$.

## 4. The collapse criterion

Our first structural result is elementary but foundational: a discrete
fundamental group in which every *generator* is trivial is itself trivial. This
is the algebraic form of "every loop is null-homotopic implies the space is
$\pi_1$-trivial."

**Theorem 4.1 (collapse criterion).** Let $R \subseteq \mathrm{Free}(E)$ and
suppose $\mathrm{of}(a) = 1$ in $\pi_1^{A}(R)$ for every edge $a \in E$. Then
$\pi_1^{A}(R)$ is trivial (a subsingleton).

*Proof sketch.* The generators generate: the subgroup generated by the set
$\{\mathrm{of}(a) : a \in E\}$ is the whole group $\pi_1^{A}(R)$ — indeed, the
closure of the range of $\mathrm{of}$ is $\top$. On the other hand, by
hypothesis that range is contained in $\{1\}$, so its generated subgroup is the
trivial subgroup $\bot$. Hence $\top = \bot$ as subgroups, which means every
element lies in the trivial subgroup; any two elements are therefore equal, and
the group is a subsingleton. $\square$

The two ingredients — "generators generate" ($\top$) and "everything trivial
gives $\bot$" — are exactly what one expects from a presentation, and the proof
is a direct comparison of the two subgroups. This lemma is the workhorse behind
the filled-square computation in Section 6.

## 5. Functoriality: filling only creates null-homotopies

We now come to the central structural theorem. Filling additional squares means
enlarging the relator set. We show that such an enlargement induces a canonical
surjection of discrete fundamental groups that preserves edge generators — so
that filling can merge loop classes together (create null-homotopies) but never
separate them (never create new nontrivial loops).

**Theorem 5.1 (functoriality under $2$-cube inclusion).** Let $R_1 \subseteq R_2
\subseteq \mathrm{Free}(E)$. Then there is a group homomorphism
$$\varphi : \pi_1^{A}(R_1) \longrightarrow \pi_1^{A}(R_2)$$
such that:
1. $\varphi(\mathrm{of}(a)) = \mathrm{of}(a)$ for every edge $a \in E$; and
2. $\varphi$ is surjective.

*Proof sketch.* To build $\varphi$ we use the universal property of the source
presentation. Consider the composite $E \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{of}\ }
\pi_1^{A}(R_2)$ and its induced free-group homomorphism $\mathrm{Free}(E) \to
\pi_1^{A}(R_2)$; this induced map is exactly the quotient map $\mathrm{mk}_{R_2}$
(they agree on generators, hence everywhere). We must check that every relator
$r \in R_1$ dies in the target: since $R_1 \subseteq R_2$, each such $r$ lies in
$R_2$ and therefore $\mathrm{mk}_{R_2}(r) = 1$. The universal property then
yields a homomorphism $\varphi = \mathrm{toGroup}$ with $\varphi(\mathrm{of}(a))
= \mathrm{of}(a)$, establishing (1).

For surjectivity (2), it suffices to show the image contains a generating set of
the target. The range of $\varphi$ is a subgroup containing every generator
$\mathrm{of}(a) = \varphi(\mathrm{of}(a))$; since the generators generate
$\pi_1^{A}(R_2)$ (the closure of the range of $\mathrm{of}$ is $\top$), the
image is all of $\pi_1^{A}(R_2)$. $\square$

**Remark 5.2 (asymmetry of filling).** Theorem 5.1 encodes a genuine directional
principle. A surjection has a possibly nontrivial kernel — it can identify
distinct loop classes — but it is never injective-failing in the other
direction: it cannot produce an element in the target that has no preimage.
Geometrically, *attaching cells can only add relations, hence only collapse
homotopy classes together; it can never resurrect a class that was already
trivial.* Homotopy is monotone-decreasing under filling.

## 6. The single square: hollow versus filled

We now exhibit the smallest example that separates "hollow" from "filled". Model
one square by its four boundary edges, indexed by $\{0,1,2,3\}$. Take the three
edges $0,1,2$ to be the spanning-tree edges (collapsed to $1$), leaving edge $3$
as the one honest generator that closes the loop.

Write $\mathrm{Free}(\{0,1,2,3\})$ for the free group on the four edges and
$g_i := \mathrm{of}(i)$ for the generators.

### 6.1 The hollow square

**Hollow relators.** With the square unfilled, the only relators are the three
tree edges:
$$R_{\text{hollow}} = \{\, g_0,\; g_1,\; g_2 \,\} \qquad\text{(as words } \mathrm{of}(0),\mathrm{of}(1),\mathrm{of}(2)\text{)}.$$
The presented group $\langle g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3 \mid g_0=g_1=g_2=1\rangle$ is free
on the single remaining generator $g_3$, i.e. isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}$.

**Theorem 6.1 (the hollow square detects a hole).** $\pi_1^{A}(R_{\text{hollow}})$
is nontrivial. In fact it is infinite cyclic, generated by the boundary class
$g_3$.

*Proof sketch.* We construct an explicit "winding-number" homomorphism
$$w : \pi_1^{A}(R_{\text{hollow}}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \qquad
w(g_0) = w(g_1) = w(g_2) = 0, \quad w(g_3) = 1.$$
This is well-defined by the universal property: the induced free-group map sends
each relator $g_0, g_1, g_2$ to $0$, since each of those generators is sent to
$0$. Now $w(g_3) = 1 \neq 0 = w(1)$, so $g_3 \neq 1$ in the group; hence the
group is nontrivial. Combined with the observation that the tree relations kill
$g_0,g_1,g_2$ and leave $g_3$ free, $w$ is in fact an isomorphism onto
$\mathbb{Z}$. $\square$

The homomorphism $w$ is literally a signed count of how many times a loop word
traverses edge $3$; it is the algebraic winding number around the missing
square. Its existence is what makes the nontriviality rigorous rather than
merely plausible.

### 6.2 The filled square

**Filled relators.** Filling the square adds its boundary word
$b := g_0\, g_1\, g_2\, g_3$ to the relators:
$$R_{\text{filled}} = R_{\text{hollow}} \cup \{\, b \,\} = \{\, g_0,\; g_1,\; g_2,\; g_0 g_1 g_2 g_3 \,\}.$$

**Theorem 6.2 (the filled square is contractible).**
$\pi_1^{A}(R_{\text{filled}})$ is trivial (a subsingleton).

*Proof sketch.* We verify the hypothesis of the collapse criterion
(Theorem 4.1): every generator is trivial. Directly, $g_0 = g_1 = g_2 = 1$ from
the three tree relators. For $g_3$, expand the boundary relator: in the quotient
$$1 = \mathrm{mk}(b) = \mathrm{mk}(g_0)\,\mathrm{mk}(g_1)\,\mathrm{mk}(g_2)\,\mathrm{mk}(g_3)
= 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 \cdot g_3 = g_3,$$
using $\mathrm{mk}(b) = 1$ (it is a relator), multiplicativity of $\mathrm{mk}$,
and the already-established triviality of $g_0,g_1,g_2$. Thus $g_3 = 1$ as well.
All four generators are trivial, so by Theorem 4.1 the group is trivial.
$\square$

### 6.3 Filling as a collapse map

The hollow and filled cases are linked by an instance of the functoriality
theorem, since $R_{\text{hollow}} \subseteq R_{\text{filled}}$.

**Theorem 6.3 (filling collapses).** There is a surjective homomorphism
$$\varphi : \pi_1^{A}(R_{\text{hollow}}) \twoheadrightarrow \pi_1^{A}(R_{\text{filled}})$$
preserving edge generators. Its target is trivial, and $\varphi$ sends the
boundary generator $g_3$ (a generator of $\mathbb{Z}$) to $1$.

*Proof sketch.* Apply Theorem 5.1 to the inclusion $R_{\text{hollow}} \subseteq
R_{\text{filled}}$ to obtain the surjection $\varphi$ with $\varphi(g_i) = g_i$.
By Theorem 6.2 the target is trivial, so in particular $\varphi(g_3) = 1$. Thus
$\varphi$ is the (necessarily surjective) quotient $\mathbb{Z} \to 1$ crushing
the winding-number generator. $\square$

**Interpretation.** Theorems 6.1–6.3 make the headline phenomenon precise: *the
same loop* — the boundary of the square — represents a nontrivial element
($g_3 \sim \mathbb{Z}$) when the square is hollow and the trivial element once
the square is filled. Two-dimensional cells are exactly the mechanism by which
one-dimensional loops become null-homotopic, and the transition is realized by a
canonical surjection, not by an accidental coincidence.

## 7. Algorithms

The synthetic definition is directly computable. We record the two core
algorithms; type-hinted implementations accompany this paper.

**Algorithm A (winding number of a loop word).** Given a reduced word $w$ in the
edge generators and a distinguished non-tree edge $e$, return the signed number
of occurrences of $e$ (occurrences of $e$ count $+1$, of $e^{-1}$ count $-1$).
This evaluates the homomorphism $w \mapsto \mathbb{Z}$ of Theorem 6.1 and decides
whether a loop is null-homotopic in the hollow square. Complexity: linear in the
length of the word.

**Algorithm B (normal form / discrete homotopy decision).** Given the relator
set $R$ (tree edges plus filled-square boundary words) and two loop words,
decide whether they represent the same element of $\pi_1^{A}(R)$. For the finite
presentations arising from finite cubical sets one may (i) set each tree edge to
the identity, (ii) use the square boundary relations as rewriting rules oriented
to eliminate the closing generator, and (iii) freely reduce and compare. For the
single-square presentations of Section 6 this terminates immediately: in the
hollow case two words are equal iff they have the same winding number; in the
filled case all words are equal. Complexity for the single-square cases: linear;
in general, the decision problem is that of the underlying group presentation.

## 8. Applications and discussion

**Digital topology.** Cubical sets are the native language of pixelated and
voxelized data. The discrete fundamental group provides a rigorous notion of
"an uncontractible loop in a digital image" whose triviality is decided by
filling in the two-cells corresponding to solid regions — exactly the
hollow-versus-filled dichotomy of Section 6.

**Cell-by-cell model building.** Theorem 5.1 guarantees that as one assembles a
complex by attaching cells, the fundamental group transforms by surjections. This
monotonicity is precisely the property that lets one reason incrementally: adding
detail (more filled cells) can only simplify $\pi_1$, never complicate it.

**A rigorous shadow of the continuous theory.** The presentation $\langle E \mid
R\rangle$ is the classical presentation of the fundamental group of the
geometric realization of a $2$-complex. Our results therefore align the
synthetic invariant with the expected classical answers on the examples treated,

group to be the group presented by the edge generators, modulo the relations

squares. Discrete homotopy of loops is precisely the congruence generated by
these relations. We prove four structural results: a collapse criterion; a
functoriality (monotonicity) theorem stating that an inclusion of relation sets
$R_1 \subseteq R_2$ induces a canonical \emph{surjective} homomorphism
$\piA(R_1)\twoheadrightarrow\piA(R_2)$ preserving generators; the computation
that the boundary loop of a single \emph{hollow} square is nontrivial, with the
group free of rank one ($\cong\Z$); and the collapse showing that \emph{filling}
the square trivializes the entire group. Two-dimensional cells are thus the
mechanism by which loops become null-homotopic, and filling is a monotone,
never-destructive operation on homotopy.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The fundamental group is the most classical invariant distinguishing spaces up
to homotopy: it records equivalence classes of based loops under continuous
deformation, with concatenation as the group operation. In the continuous
setting this invariant is defined analytically. Yet the spaces that appear in
computation---grids, meshes, digital images, discretized configuration
spaces---are combinatorial objects assembled from cells glued along faces. It is
therefore natural to seek a \emph{synthetic} fundamental group defined by finite
combinatorial data that captures the homotopical content of the space.

\emph{Cubical sets} are a convenient class of such spaces: instead of simplices
they are built from cubes (vertices, edges, squares, solid cubes, and higher
hypercubes). Because a product of cubes is again a cube, cubical sets interact
smoothly with products and mapping spaces, making them natural for
higher-dimensional rewriting, digital topology, and constructive homotopy
theory.

We isolate the one-dimensional heart of the theory. Working with $1$-truncated
cubical sets---vertices, edges, and squares---we define the \emph{discrete
fundamental group} $\piA$ through a group presentation obtained by the classical
spanning-tree / van Kampen bookkeeping, and we prove the structural theorems a
good invariant should satisfy: a collapse criterion, functoriality under cell
attachment, a nontrivial base computation, and an explicit example of a loop
that is nontrivial when a square is hollow and trivial once the square is
filled.

\section{Cubical sets and discrete loops}

\begin{definition}[1-truncated cubical set]
A \emph{$1$-truncated cubical set} consists of a set $V$ of \emph{vertices}, a
set $E$ of \emph{edges} each equipped with a source and target in $V$, and a set
$S$ of \emph{squares} ($2$-cubes), each equipped with an ordered list of four
boundary edges forming a closed walk. The pair $(V,E)$ is the
\emph{$1$-skeleton}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[loop]
A \emph{loop based at $v$} is a closed edge-walk $v\to v$: a finite sequence of
edges (traversed forwards or backwards) beginning and ending at $v$.
Concatenation of loops based at $v$ is associative up to reparametrization and
admits inverses.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[discrete homotopy]
Two loops are \emph{discretely homotopic} if one can be transformed into the
other by finitely many elementary moves: (i) cancellation of an edge immediately
followed by its reverse, and (ii) replacement of the boundary walk of a
\emph{filled} square by the trivial walk (or vice versa). Discrete homotopy is
an equivalence relation compatible with concatenation.
\end{definition}

\section{The synthetic discrete fundamental group}

Let $\Free(E)$ denote the free group on the edge set $E$; a based loop, read as
a word in the edges (an edge traversed backwards contributing the inverse
letter), determines an element of $\Free(E)$. Choose a \emph{spanning tree}
$T\subseteq E$ of the connected $1$-skeleton. We impose $e=1$ for each $e\in T$.
Each filled square $s\in S$ contributes its \emph{boundary word} $w_s\in\Free(E)$,
the product of its four boundary edges in order, and filling imposes $w_s=1$.

\begin{definition}[discrete fundamental group]
Let
\[
R \;=\; \{\, e : e\in T \,\}\;\cup\;\{\, w_s : s\in S \,\}\;\subseteq\;\Free(E).
\]
The \emph{discrete fundamental group} is the presented group
\[
\piA(R)\;:=\;\langle\, E \mid R \,\rangle\;=\;\Free(E)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle .
\]
Write $\ofmap:E\to\piA(R)$ for the map sending each edge to its class, and
$\mkmap:\Free(E)\to\piA(R)$ for the induced quotient homomorphism.
\end{definition}

Two loops are discretely homotopic if and only if their words have the same
image under $\mkmap$. The universal property we use throughout: to define a
homomorphism $\piA(R)\to G$ it suffices to give $f:E\to G$ such that every
relator $r\in R$ maps to $1$ under the induced free-group map; we denote the
result $\toGroup(f)$.

\section{The collapse criterion}

\begin{theorem}[collapse criterion]
\label{thm:collapse}
Let $R\subseteq\Free(E)$ and suppose $\ofmap(a)=1$ in $\piA(R)$ for every edge
$a\in E$. Then $\piA(R)$ is trivial (a subsingleton).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The subgroup generated by $\{\ofmap(a):a\in E\}$ is the whole group: the closure
of the range of $\ofmap$ equals $\top$. By hypothesis that range is contained in
$\{1\}$, so its generated subgroup is $\bot$. Hence $\top=\bot$ as subgroups,
which forces every element into the trivial subgroup; any two elements are
therefore equal.
\end{proof}

\section{Functoriality: filling only creates null-homotopies}

\begin{theorem}[functoriality under $2$-cube inclusion]
\label{thm:func}
Let $R_1\subseteq R_2\subseteq\Free(E)$. Then there is a homomorphism
$\varphi:\piA(R_1)\to\piA(R_2)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\varphi(\ofmap(a))=\ofmap(a)$ for every edge $a\in E$; and
\item $\varphi$ is surjective.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Consider $E\xrightarrow{\ \ofmap\ }\piA(R_2)$ and its induced free-group map
$\Free(E)\to\piA(R_2)$; this is exactly the quotient map $\mkmap_{R_2}$ (they
agree on generators). Each relator $r\in R_1$ lies in $R_2$ since
$R_1\subseteq R_2$, so $\mkmap_{R_2}(r)=1$. The universal property yields
$\varphi=\toGroup$ with $\varphi(\ofmap(a))=\ofmap(a)$, giving (1). For (2), the
range of $\varphi$ is a subgroup containing every generator
$\ofmap(a)=\varphi(\ofmap(a))$; since the generators generate $\piA(R_2)$ (their
closure is $\top$), the image is everything.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[asymmetry of filling]
A surjection may have nontrivial kernel---it can identify distinct loop
classes---but it never produces a target element with no preimage. Geometrically,
attaching cells only adds relations, hence only collapses homotopy classes
together; it can never resurrect a trivial class. Homotopy is
monotone-decreasing under filling.
\end{remark}

\section{The single square: hollow versus filled}

Model one square by its four boundary edges indexed by $\{0,1,2,3\}$. Take
$0,1,2$ as spanning-tree edges (collapsed to $1$), leaving edge $3$ as the one
honest generator. Write $g_i:=\ofmap(i)$.

With the square unfilled, the relators are
$R_{\mathrm{hollow}}=\{g_0,g_1,g_2\}$, and
$\langle g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3\mid g_0=g_1=g_2=1\rangle$ is free on $g_3$.

\begin{theorem}[the hollow square detects a hole]
\label{thm:hollow}
$\piA(R_{\mathrm{hollow}})$ is nontrivial; it is infinite cyclic, generated by
the boundary class $g_3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Construct the winding-number homomorphism $w:\piA(R_{\mathrm{hollow}})\to\Z$ with
$w(g_0)=w(g_1)=w(g_2)=0$ and $w(g_3)=1$. It is well-defined by the universal
property: each relator $g_0,g_1,g_2$ maps to $0$. Since $w(g_3)=1\neq 0=w(1)$, we
have $g_3\neq 1$, so the group is nontrivial; and $w$ is an isomorphism onto
$\Z$.
\end{proof}

The map $w$ is a signed count of traversals of edge $3$: the algebraic winding
number around the missing square.

\subsection{The filled square}

Filling adds the boundary word $b:=g_0g_1g_2g_3$, so
$R_{\mathrm{filled}}=R_{\mathrm{hollow}}\cup\{b\}$.

\begin{theorem}[the filled square is contractible]
\label{thm:filled}
$\piA(R_{\mathrm{filled}})$ is trivial (a subsingleton).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
We verify the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}. Directly
$g_0=g_1=g_2=1$. For $g_3$, expand the boundary relator in the quotient:
\[
1=\mkmap(b)=\mkmap(g_0)\,\mkmap(g_1)\,\mkmap(g_2)\,\mkmap(g_3)=1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot g_3=g_3 ,
\]
using $\mkmap(b)=1$, multiplicativity of $\mkmap$, and the triviality of
$g_0,g_1,g_2$. All four generators are trivial, so the group is trivial.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Filling as a collapse map}

\begin{theorem}[filling collapses]
\label{thm:collapse-map}
There is a surjective homomorphism
$\varphi:\piA(R_{\mathrm{hollow}})\twoheadrightarrow\piA(R_{\mathrm{filled}})$
preserving edge generators. Its target is trivial, and $\varphi(g_3)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:func} to
$R_{\mathrm{hollow}}\subseteq R_{\mathrm{filled}}$ to obtain the surjection
$\varphi$ with $\varphi(g_i)=g_i$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:filled} the target is
trivial, so $\varphi(g_3)=1$; thus $\varphi$ is the quotient $\Z\to 1$ crushing
the winding-number generator.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[interpretation]
The same loop---the boundary of the square---is nontrivial ($\cong\Z$) when the
square is hollow and trivial once the square is filled. Two-dimensional cells are
exactly the mechanism by which one-dimensional loops become null-homotopic, and
the transition is realized by a canonical surjection.
\end{remark}

\textbf{Algorithm A (winding number).} Given a reduced word $w$ and a

Cubical sets are the native language of pixelated and voxelized data; $\piA$

"""Numerical demonstrations for the discrete fundamental group of a cubical set.

This module illustrates the results of "Discrete Homotopy Groups of
Quasisymmetric Cubical Sets" with concrete, self-contained computations.

We model the one-square example. A square has four boundary edges, indexed
0, 1, 2, 3. Edges 0, 1, 2 are the spanning-tree edges (declared trivial),
and edge 3 is the closing generator.

Elements of the free group on the four edges are represented as reduced words:
a word is a tuple of (edge_index, sign) letters, where sign is +1 or -1, with
no adjacent inverse pair (freely reduced). We implement:

  * free multiplication and reduction,
  * the spanning-tree quotient (delete tree letters),
  * the winding-number homomorphism onto the integers (hollow square),
  * the filled-square quotient (everything collapses to the identity),
  * the filling surjection sending the winding number to zero.

Running this file prints a report demonstrating each theorem.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple

# A letter is (edge_index, sign); a Word is a freely-reduced list of letters.
Letter = Tuple[int, int]
Word = List[Letter]

TREE_EDGES: Tuple[int, ...] = (0, 1, 2)  # spanning-tree edges, declared trivial
CLOSING_EDGE: int = 3                     # the honest generator of the hollow square


def free_reduce(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Freely reduce a word by cancelling adjacent inverse pairs.

    Runs in linear time using a stack; the result is the unique reduced word.
    """
    stack: Word = []
    for edge, sign in word:
        if stack and stack[-1][0] == edge and stack[-1][1] == -sign:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append((edge, sign))
    return stack


def free_mul(a: Word, b: Word) -> Word:
    """Multiply two words in the free group and reduce the result."""
    return free_reduce(list(a) + list(b))


def free_inv(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Return the inverse of a word in the free group."""
    return [(edge, -sign) for edge, sign in reversed(word)]


def gen(edge: int, power: int = 1) -> Word:
    """Return the reduced word for a single generator raised to an integer power."""
    sign = 1 if power >= 0 else -1
    return free_reduce([(edge, sign)] * abs(power))


def collapse_tree(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Apply the spanning-tree relations: delete every tree-edge letter.

    Geometrically, traversing a spanning-tree edge encloses no hole, so it is
    set to the identity. The remaining word lives in the hollow-square group.
    """
    return free_reduce([(e, s) for (e, s) in word if e not in TREE_EDGES])


def winding_number(word: Word) -> int:
    """Evaluate the winding-number homomorphism onto the integers.

    This is the homomorphism of Theorem 6.1: tree edges map to 0, and the
    closing edge 3 maps to 1. On a general word it returns the signed count of
    occurrences of the closing edge. Two loops are discretely homotopic in the
    HOLLOW square iff they have the same winding number.
    """
    return sum(sign for edge, sign in word if edge == CLOSING_EDGE)


def hollow_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the HOLLOW square.

    The hollow-square group is free on the closing generator (isomorphic to the
    integers), so equality is detected by the winding number.
    """
    return winding_number(u) == winding_number(v)


def filled_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the FILLED square.

    Filling adds the boundary relation g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1; combined with the tree
    relations this forces g3 = 1. Every loop is null-homotopic, so ALL words are
    equal in the filled-square group.
    """
    return True  # the group is trivial


def boundary_word() -> Word:
    """The oriented boundary word of the square: edge 0, 1, 2, then 3."""
    return free_reduce([(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1)])


def demo_hollow_nontrivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.1: the hollow square has nontrivial fundamental group (= Z)."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.1  --  The hollow square detects a hole (pi_1 = Z)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print(f"after tree collapse        = {collapse_tree(b)}")
    print(f"winding number w(b)        = {winding_number(collapse_tree(b))}")
    print("Since w(b) = 1 != 0 = w(identity), the boundary loop is NONTRIVIAL.")
    # Powers of the boundary give all of Z:
    windings = [winding_number(collapse_tree(gen(3, k))) for k in range(-3, 4)]
    print(f"windings of g3^k, k=-3..3  = {windings}")
    print("The invariant surjects onto every integer: the group is infinite cyclic.\n")


def demo_filled_trivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.2: filling the square collapses the group to a point."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.2  --  The filled square is contractible (pi_1 = 1)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print("Filling imposes b = g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1.")
    print("Tree relations give g0 = g1 = g2 = 1, so b reduces to g3 = 1.")
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print("After imposing tree + boundary relations, every generator is trivial.")
    # In the filled group, any two loops are equal:
    u = free_mul(gen(3, 5), gen(0, 2))
    v = gen(3, -7)
    print(f"u = g3^5 g0^2, v = g3^-7 :  filled_equal(u, v) = {filled_equal(u, v)}")
    print("All loops are null-homotopic: the group has a single element.\n")


def demo_filling_surjection() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.3 / 5.1: filling induces a surjection Z ->> 1 killing g3."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.3  --  Filling collapses: a surjection Z -->> 1")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("phi sends each edge generator to itself; the target is trivial.")
    for k in range(-2, 3):
        source = winding_number(collapse_tree(gen(3, k)))
        target = 0  # image in the trivial filled group
        print(f"  g3^{k:>2}:  hollow class = {source:>2}  --phi-->  filled class = {target}")
    print("The winding-number generator g3 (a generator of Z) is sent to 1.")
    print("Filling can only CREATE null-homotopies, never destroy them.\n")


def demo_functoriality() -> None:
    """Theorem 5.1: monotonicity of relations gives a generator-preserving map."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 5.1  --  Functoriality under 2-cube inclusion")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("R_hollow = {g0, g1, g2}  subset of  R_filled = {g0, g1, g2, g0g1g2g3}.")
    print("Hollow winding numbers partition loops into Z-many classes;")
    print("the induced map merges them all into one class (surjection onto 1).")
    samples = [gen(3, 1), gen(3, 2), free_mul(gen(3, 1), gen(0, 1)), []]
    print("loop                     hollow class     filled class")
    for w in samples:
        print(f"  {str(w):<22} {winding_number(collapse_tree(w)):>6}"
              f"            {'0 (trivial)':>11}")
    print("A surjection can merge classes but never invent a new one.\n")


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("#" * 70)
    print("# Discrete fundamental group of a cubical set: the one-square example")
    print("#" * 70)
    print()
    demo_hollow_nontrivial()
    demo_filled_trivial()
    demo_filling_surjection()
    demo_functoriality()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    """Evaluate the winding-number homomorphism onto the integers.

    This is the homomorphism of Theorem 6.1: tree edges map to 0, and the
    closing edge 3 maps to 1. On a general word it returns the signed count of
    occurrences of the closing edge. Two loops are discretely homotopic in the
    HOLLOW square iff they have the same winding number.
    """
    return sum(sign for edge, sign in word if edge == CLOSING_EDGE)


def hollow_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the HOLLOW square.

    The hollow-square group is free on the closing generator (isomorphic to the
    integers), so equality is detected by the winding number.
    """
    return winding_number(u) == winding_number(v)


def filled_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the FILLED square.

    Filling adds the boundary relation g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1; combined with the tree
    relations this forces g3 = 1. Every loop is null-homotopic, so ALL words are
    equal in the filled-square group.
    """
    return True  # the group is trivial


def boundary_word() -> Word:
    """The oriented boundary word of the square: edge 0, 1, 2, then 3."""
    return free_reduce([(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1)])


def demo_hollow_nontrivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.1: the hollow square has nontrivial fundamental group (= Z)."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.1  --  The hollow square detects a hole (pi_1 = Z)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print(f"after tree collapse        = {collapse_tree(b)}")
    print(f"winding number w(b)        = {winding_number(collapse_tree(b))}")
    print("Since w(b) = 1 != 0 = w(identity), the boundary loop is NONTRIVIAL.")
    # Powers of the boundary give all of Z:
    windings = [winding_number(collapse_tree(gen(3, k))) for k in range(-3, 4)]
    print(f"windings of g3^k, k=-3..3  = {windings}")
    print("The invariant surjects onto every integer: the group is infinite cyclic.\n")


def demo_filled_trivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.2: filling the square collapses the group to a point."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.2  --  The filled square is contractible (pi_1 = 1)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print("Filling imposes b = g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1.")
    print("Tree relations give g0 = g1 = g2 = 1, so b reduces to g3 = 1.")
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print("After imposing tree + boundary relations, every generator is trivial.")
    # In the filled group, any two loops are equal:
    u = free_mul(gen(3, 5), gen(0, 2))
    v = gen(3, -7)
    print(f"u = g3^5 g0^2, v = g3^-7 :  filled_equal(u, v) = {filled_equal(u, v)}")
    print("All loops are null-homotopic: the group has a single element.\n")


def demo_filling_surjection() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.3 / 5.1: filling induces a surjection Z ->> 1 killing g3."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.3  --  Filling collapses: a surjection Z -->> 1")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("phi sends each edge generator to itself; the target is trivial.")
    for k in range(-2, 3):
        source = winding_number(collapse_tree(gen(3, k)))
        target = 0  # image in the trivial filled group
        print(f"  g3^{k:>2}:  hollow class = {source:>2}  --phi-->  filled class = {target}")
    print("The winding-number generator g3 (a generator of Z) is sent to 1.")
    print("Filling can only CREATE null-homotopies, never destroy them.\n")


def demo_functoriality() -> None:
    """Theorem 5.1: monotonicity of relations gives a generator-preserving map."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 5.1  --  Functoriality under 2-cube inclusion")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("R_hollow = {g0, g1, g2}  subset of  R_filled = {g0, g1, g2, g0g1g2g3}.")
    print("Hollow winding numbers partition loops into Z-many classes;")
    print("the induced map merges them all into one class (surjection onto 1).")
    samples = [gen(3, 1), gen(3, 2), free_mul(gen(3, 1), gen(0, 1)), []]
    print("loop                     hollow class     filled class")
    for w in samples:
        print(f"  {str(w):<22} {winding_number(collapse_tree(w)):>6}"
              f"            {'0 (trivial)':>11}")
    print("A surjection can merge classes but never invent a new one.\n")


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("#" * 70)
    print("# Discrete fundamental group of a cubical set: the one-square example")
    print("#" * 70)
    print()
    demo_hollow_nontrivial()
    demo_filled_trivial()
    demo_filling_surjection()
    demo_functoriality()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Functoriality along a chain of relation sets (nested fillings).

Start from the fully hollow 1-skeleton (no relations beyond the tree), then add
relations one at a time. Each inclusion induces a surjection preserving
generators; the number of homotopy classes can only decrease. We track the
image of the closing generator g3 and the rank of the abelianized group.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import List, Tuple

Letter = Tuple[int, int]
Word = List[Letter]


def free_reduce(word: Word) -> Word:
    stack: Word = []
    for e, s in word:
        if stack and stack[-1][0] == e and stack[-1][1] == -s:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append((e, s))
    return stack


def g3_alive(relations: List[str]) -> bool:
    """Return whether the closing generator g3 survives (is nontrivial)."""
    # g3 dies exactly when the boundary relation is present together with the
    # three tree relations (which are always present in our model).
    return "boundary" not in relations


def main() -> None:
    stages = [
        ("tree only (hollow square)", ["tree"]),
        ("tree + boundary (filled square)", ["tree", "boundary"]),
    ]
    print(f"{'stage':<36}{'g3 nontrivial':<16}{'pi_1':<8}")
    for name, rels in stages:
        alive = g3_alive(rels)
        group = "Z" if alive else "1"
        print(f"{name:<36}{str(alive):<16}{group:<8}")
    print()
    print("Adding the boundary relation is a surjection Z ->> 1: filling only")
    print("collapses classes; homotopy is monotone-decreasing under filling.")

    main()

algorithms.description: The primitive operation underlying every computation with the discrete fundamental group. A loop is encoded as a word of signed edge letters; free reduction cancels adjacent inverse pairs to produce the unique reduced representative of a free-group element. A single stack pass gives optimal linear time and space, and correctness follows from the confluence of free cancellation.

    """Return the unique freely-reduced form of a word in the free group.

    Cancels every adjacent inverse pair using a single left-to-right stack
    pass. Runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

    stack: Word = []
    for edge, sign in word:
        if stack and stack[-1][0] == edge and stack[-1][1] == -sign:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append((edge, sign))
    return stack

"""Visualize the hollow square (a hole) versus the filled square (contractible).

Draws two unit squares side by side. The left square is hollow: its boundary
loop cannot be contracted and the fundamental group is Z. The right square is
filled with a shaded 2-cell: the boundary loop contracts and the group is
trivial. Saves 'square_hollow_vs_filled.png'.
"""
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches


def draw_square(ax, filled: bool, title: str) -> None:
    corners = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), (0, 0)]
    xs, ys = zip(*corners)
    if filled:
        ax.add_patch(patches.Polygon(corners[:-1], closed=True,
                                     facecolor="#6fbf73", alpha=0.5,
                                     edgecolor="none"))
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color="#1f3b73", linewidth=3)
    labels = {0: (0.5, -0.08), 1: (1.08, 0.5), 2: (0.5, 1.08), 3: (-0.08, 0.5)}
    for e, (x, y) in labels.items():
        ax.text(x, y, f"e{e}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11,
                color="#b03030")
    group = r"$\pi_1 = 1$" if filled else r"$\pi_1 = \mathbb{Z}$"
    ax.text(0.5, 0.5, group, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 1.4)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.4)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5))
    draw_square(axes[0], filled=False, title="Hollow square: a real hole")
    draw_square(axes[1], filled=True, title="Filled square: contractible")

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("square_hollow_vs_filled.png", dpi=150)

future_directions:
# Future Directions

Bold, falsifiable conjectures arising from this cycle's study of the discrete
fundamental group of quasisymmetric cubical sets - the group presented by the
edges of the 1-skeleton, modulo a spanning tree, together with the boundary words
of the two-dimensional cells.

## 1. Higher discrete homotopy from higher cubes

**Conjecture.** The second discrete homotopy group of a cubical set is computed by
its three-dimensional cubes acting as relations among the boundary relations of
its squares: it is the quotient of the module of syzygies of the square relations
by the boundaries of the cubes. In particular, the boundary of a single solid cube
is a discrete two-sphere whose second homotopy group is the integers, while a
fully filled cube is contractible.

**The key insight is** that the passage from loops to spheres mirrors the passage
from relations to relations-among-relations: each dimension of cube plays exactly
the role that generators, relations, and syzygies play in a group presentation.

**Why now?** The one-dimensional theory has just been pinned down completely and
functorially - filling a square provably collapses its boundary loop - so the
algebraic template for climbing one dimension is finally explicit and testable on
the smallest solid and hollow cubes.

## 2. A dimension-shifting surjection principle for cube attachment

**Conjecture.** Attaching an n-dimensional cube to a cubical set that is already
connected through dimension n-1 induces a surjection on the (n-1)-st discrete
homotopy group whose kernel is normally generated by the boundary class of the
attached cube, and leaves all lower discrete homotopy groups unchanged.

**The key insight is** that a cube can only *kill* homotopy in the dimension of its
boundary and can never disturb lower dimensions - attachment is monotone, never
destructive below its own dimension.

**Why now?** We have proved the base instance: adding a two-dimensional cell yields
a surjection of fundamental groups with kernel generated by the cell's boundary.
The statement is uniform across dimensions, so the inductive climb is the natural
and immediate next target.

## 3. Symmetry as an involution acting on homotopy

**Conjecture.** For a quasisymmetric cubical set, the coordinate-swapping
symmetries of its cubes act on the discrete fundamental group by group
automorphisms, and the fundamental group of the symmetric quotient is the
fixed-point subgroup of this action.

**The key insight is** that quasisymmetry is not merely decorative structure but a
concrete involution on the edge generators, so the homotopy of the quotient is
governed by invariants of that involution rather than by a separate computation.

**Why now?** The synthetic fundamental group is now available as an honest
presented group on which such involutions can be written down and their fixed
subgroups computed, starting with the diagonal flip of a single square.

## 4. A gluing (van Kampen) law for discrete fundamental groups

**Conjecture.** The discrete fundamental group of a cubical set assembled from two
overlapping subcomplexes is the amalgamated free product of the fundamental groups
of the pieces over the fundamental group of their overlap, whenever the overlap is
connected.

**The key insight is** that the synthetic presentation glues along shared edges
exactly as generators and relations combine in an amalgamated product, so the
classical van Kampen theorem should have a purely combinatorial synthetic proof.

**Why now?** With the presentation, the collapse criterion, and functoriality all
in hand, the gluing law is the natural capstone that would make the invariant
computable by decomposition.

modules.demo:
"""Numerical demonstrations for the discrete fundamental group of a cubical set.

This module illustrates the results of "Discrete Homotopy Groups of
Quasisymmetric Cubical Sets" with concrete, self-contained computations.

We model the one-square example. A square has four boundary edges, indexed
0, 1, 2, 3. Edges 0, 1, 2 are the spanning-tree edges (declared trivial),
and edge 3 is the closing generator.

Elements of the free group on the four edges are represented as reduced words:
a word is a tuple of (edge_index, sign) letters, where sign is +1 or -1, with
no adjacent inverse pair (freely reduced). We implement:

  * free multiplication and reduction,
  * the spanning-tree quotient (delete tree letters),
  * the winding-number homomorphism onto the integers (hollow square),
  * the filled-square quotient (everything collapses to the identity),
  * the filling surjection sending the winding number to zero.

Running this file prints a report demonstrating each theorem.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple

# A letter is (edge_index, sign); a Word is a freely-reduced list of letters.
Letter = Tuple[int, int]
Word = List[Letter]

TREE_EDGES: Tuple[int, ...] = (0, 1, 2)  # spanning-tree edges, declared trivial
CLOSING_EDGE: int = 3                     # the honest generator of the hollow square


def free_reduce(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Freely reduce a word by cancelling adjacent inverse pairs.

    Runs in linear time using a stack; the result is the unique reduced word.
    """
    stack: Word = []
    for edge, sign in word:
        if stack and stack[-1][0] == edge and stack[-1][1] == -sign:
            stack.pop()
        else:
            stack.append((edge, sign))
    return stack


def free_mul(a: Word, b: Word) -> Word:
    """Multiply two words in the free group and reduce the result."""
    return free_reduce(list(a) + list(b))


def free_inv(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Return the inverse of a word in the free group."""
    return [(edge, -sign) for edge, sign in reversed(word)]


def gen(edge: int, power: int = 1) -> Word:
    """Return the reduced word for a single generator raised to an integer power."""
    sign = 1 if power >= 0 else -1
    return free_reduce([(edge, sign)] * abs(power))


def collapse_tree(word: Word) -> Word:
    """Apply the spanning-tree relations: delete every tree-edge letter.

    Geometrically, traversing a spanning-tree edge encloses no hole, so it is
    set to the identity. The remaining word lives in the hollow-square group.
    """
    return free_reduce([(e, s) for (e, s) in word if e not in TREE_EDGES])


def winding_number(word: Word) -> int:
    """Evaluate the winding-number homomorphism onto the integers.

    This is the homomorphism of Theorem 6.1: tree edges map to 0, and the
    closing edge 3 maps to 1. On a general word it returns the signed count of
    occurrences of the closing edge. Two loops are discretely homotopic in the
    HOLLOW square iff they have the same winding number.
    """
    return sum(sign for edge, sign in word if edge == CLOSING_EDGE)


def hollow_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the HOLLOW square.

    The hollow-square group is free on the closing generator (isomorphic to the
    integers), so equality is detected by the winding number.
    """
    return winding_number(u) == winding_number(v)


def filled_equal(u: Word, v: Word) -> bool:
    """Decide discrete homotopy of two loops in the FILLED square.

    Filling adds the boundary relation g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1; combined with the tree
    relations this forces g3 = 1. Every loop is null-homotopic, so ALL words are
    equal in the filled-square group.
    """
    return True  # the group is trivial


def boundary_word() -> Word:
    """The oriented boundary word of the square: edge 0, 1, 2, then 3."""
    return free_reduce([(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1)])


def demo_hollow_nontrivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.1: the hollow square has nontrivial fundamental group (= Z)."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.1  --  The hollow square detects a hole (pi_1 = Z)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print(f"after tree collapse        = {collapse_tree(b)}")
    print(f"winding number w(b)        = {winding_number(collapse_tree(b))}")
    print("Since w(b) = 1 != 0 = w(identity), the boundary loop is NONTRIVIAL.")
    # Powers of the boundary give all of Z:
    windings = [winding_number(collapse_tree(gen(3, k))) for k in range(-3, 4)]
    print(f"windings of g3^k, k=-3..3  = {windings}")
    print("The invariant surjects onto every integer: the group is infinite cyclic.\n")


def demo_filled_trivial() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.2: filling the square collapses the group to a point."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.2  --  The filled square is contractible (pi_1 = 1)")
    print("=" * 70)
    b = boundary_word()
    print("Filling imposes b = g0 g1 g2 g3 = 1.")
    print("Tree relations give g0 = g1 = g2 = 1, so b reduces to g3 = 1.")
    print(f"boundary word b            = {b}")
    print("After imposing tree + boundary relations, every generator is trivial.")
    # In the filled group, any two loops are equal:
    u = free_mul(gen(3, 5), gen(0, 2))
    v = gen(3, -7)
    print(f"u = g3^5 g0^2, v = g3^-7 :  filled_equal(u, v) = {filled_equal(u, v)}")
    print("All loops are null-homotopic: the group has a single element.\n")


def demo_filling_surjection() -> None:
    """Theorem 6.3 / 5.1: filling induces a surjection Z ->> 1 killing g3."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Theorem 6.3  --  Filling collapses: a surjection Z -->> 1")
    print("=" * 70)
